program_meta.program_name: CRITICAL STRUCTURAL FINDING, read first: University of Toronto Department of Computer Science offers THREE distinct graduate streams that must not be conflated. (1) MSc (thesis-based, 16 months) - VERBATIM from the MSc page: 'International applicants are not considered for the MSc in Computer Science... International applicants considering applying to graduate programs in Computer Science are strongly encouraged to apply to either the Master of Science in Applied Computing or the Direct-Entry PhD Program.' Akshat is an Indian citizen with an Indian bachelor's degree, i.e. an international applicant - the research-track MSc is CLOSED to him, full stop. (2) MScAC (Master of Science in Applied Computing) - 16 months, 8 months coursework + 8-month paid applied-research internship at a partner company, 7 selectable concentrations (incl. Artificial Intelligence, AI in Healthcare); explicitly NOT a faculty-supervised research degree - 'professional/project-based' per the user's own framing, industry-partnered, administered via mscac.utoronto.ca (separate application system, not covered by CS's how-to-apply page). (3) Direct-Entry PhD - 'intended for international students' (verbatim, from the PhD page, which also states 'Domestic students without an appropriate master's degree should apply to the MSc program and enter the PhD upon completion' - the mirror-image statement confirming MSc is a domestic-only funnel into the PhD). CONCLUSION: for Akshat, the realistic UofT CS research-degree pathway is the Direct-Entry PhD, not the MSc, despite the user's stated target of 'MSc CS'. This file therefore reports facts for the Direct-Entry PhD (research/thesis, faculty-supervised) as the closest analogue to what the user asked to verify, and separately for MScAC, and flags the MSc research-track facts (SOP/LOR/deadline mechanics) for completeness even though Akshat cannot apply to it.

Describe any original research that you have done: the results, their importance, your role in the research, and your role in writing any publications arising from this research. If you have specific research plans, outline them here... Include the names of any faculty members whom you are particularly interested in working with.' program_meta.advisor_model: CRITICAL AND UNUSUAL - VERIFY BEFORE WRITING ANY SOP. VERBATIM (identical language on both MSc and PhD pages): 'All MSc/PhD students are assigned a supervisor or research group based on the research interests indicated in their application.' The How-to-Apply page adds: 'On the application you will be asked to rank your research interests and faculty members with whom you would like to work.' This means UofT CS applicants RANK preferred faculty/research areas AS PART OF THE APPLICATION FORM ITSELF - it is not merely an SOP-mention convention as at UT Austin/Berkeley, it is a structured field the admissions committee and individual faculty use to route applications. This is the 'pre-matched or ranked by potential supervisors' mechanism the user asked to verify - CONFIRMED, and it is more formal/structured at UofT than at most peer programs on this list. It does NOT necessarily mean a specific professor must pre-commit before an offer is made (that is not stated), but strong, specific, well-targeted faculty-name-dropping in both the SOP and the ranked list is structurally more important here than elsewhere. No explicit 'do you need a professor to agree before applying' FAQ answer was found (unlike Purdue's explicit 'No' or Penn's explicit 'You may contact faculty to identify a PI') - GAP: whether informal pre-application contact changes routing odds is unconfirmed either way.

program_meta.notes: VECTOR INSTITUTE: confirmed as a cross-institutional AI research institute headquartered in Toronto with which many UofT CS faculty hold Faculty Member / CIFAR AI Chair / Research Director status (Krishnan, Grosse, Duvenaud, Raffel, Maddison, Fidler, Ba, Zemel all carry Vector titles per their own pages). Vector affiliation flows FROM the UofT faculty appointment - it is not a separate admission route for MSc/PhD students, and no UofT CS page independently verified this pass states that admitted MSc students (were the MSc open to Akshat) get automatic Vector status; this is a common misconception worth flagging - Vector Institute has its own separately-administered 'Vector Scholarship in AI' funding for students already admitted to a partner university's grad program, not a parallel admissions channel. RED FLAG PATTERN CONFIRMED PER USER'S WARNING: at least three names the user asked about show exactly the 'affiliated-but-not-really-here' pattern - Razvan Pascanu does NOT appear anywhere in the full UofT CS faculty directory (Research Stream, Cross-Appointed, Status-Only, or Adjunct) - he is NOT a UofT contact of any kind; do not name him in any UofT-facing SOP. David Duvenaud's own homepage states VERBATIM 'I'm not taking new students' and describes an 'extended sabbatical on the Alignment Science team at Anthropic' - his research has visibly pivoted from probabilistic/generative modeling to AGI governance and AI safety since roughly 2024. faculty.department: Department of Computer Science, jointly with Laboratory Medicine and Pathobiology
faculty.lab: rgklab (Vector Institute); Canada CIFAR AI Chair, Tier II Canada Research Chair in Computational Medicine
faculty.research_areas: Machine learning for healthcare and biology; deep generative modeling (diffusion/masked discrete diffusion); causal machine learning and causal foundation models; probabilistic inference; time-series and survival modeling; detecting model failure/distribution shift without labels.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's DDPM-pretraining result is fundamentally a transfer-of-a-learned-generative-prior question - it works for liver, fails (worse than random init) for kidney, and he has no principled account of why. Krishnan's 'Beyond Masked and Unmasked: Discrete Diffusion Models via Partial Masking' (NeurIPS 2025) and his broader generative-modeling thread ask exactly what structure a diffusion-style prior needs to capture to transfer reliably, and his 'Reliably Detecting Model Failures in Deployment Without Labels' (D3M, NeurIPS 2025) is the deployment-side version of Akshat's core finding - that a model can silently fail on a structurally-similar-looking input (kidney vs. liver) without any labeled signal to catch it.
faculty.key_paper_1: Beyond Masked and Unmasked: Discrete Diffusion Models via Partial Masking. NeurIPS, 2025.
faculty.key_paper_2: Reliably Detecting Model Failures in Deployment Without Labels (D3M). NeurIPS, 2025. (See also: CausalPFN: Amortized Causal Effect Estimation via In-Context Learning, NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight.)
faculty.taking_students: Group is large and clearly actively recruiting/funded - lists 8 current PhD students, postdocs and MSc students as of the site's last update (16 Aug 2026), multiple 2025-2026 NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR papers. No explicit 'currently closed' notice found. Verified 2026-08-28.
faculty.contact_policy: Not stated directly on the main page; a 'Joining the Lab' link exists at https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~rahulgk/links/joining.html but its content was not fetched this pass - GAP, read before contacting.
faculty.email: not listed as a plain address on the homepage (contact via department directory: rahulgk@cs.toronto.edu, per the faculty directory listing)
faculty.email_angle: Your D3M work detects model failure in deployment without labels; I have an unresolved case of exactly that failure mode in miniature - a diffusion-pretrained encoder that transfers cleanly for liver segmentation but drops below a random-init baseline for kidney - and no labeled signal in my own pipeline would have caught it in advance.
faculty.notes: Best overall fit found at UofT: direct topical overlap with interests C and D (generative pretraining, structured/uncertain prediction), active and clearly funded group, no red flags (fully UofT/Vector-based, not primarily employed elsewhere). Read the 'Joining the Lab' page before contacting - not yet verified in this pass.

Maddison's stated current research direction, VERBATIM, is 'algorithms that learn from data or verifiers to make good predictions in stubbornly complex settings... data is scarce and verification signals are expensive' - a near-exact restatement of the constraint Akshat's spine and polyp studies operate under, and his co-authored 'Experts Don't Cheat: Learning What You Don't Know By Predicting Pairs' (ICML 2024) gives a principled, provably-correct alternative to the hand-tuned confidence/MC-dropout filter Akshat built by trial and error.
